subject: Copywriting
title: Hermès: Craft as Narrative
description: A micro-lesson that makes Hermès: Craft as Narrative usable.

hook.text: Hermès describes its artisans as 'hands.' 'Each bag passes through 18 pairs of hands.' The craft is the story.

buildup.text: The brand's copy focuses on process: leather selection, hand-stitching, saddle-stitching inherited from horse harness.

discovery.text: Hermès artisans train for 5 years before touching a Birkin bag.

twist.text: By centering artisans rather than celebrities, Hermès makes you feel you're paying for human mastery, not brand markup.

climax.text: Hermès proves that process storytelling can justify any price. When you understand the craft, the cost feels earned.

punchline.text: 18 pairs of hands, 5 years of training. The craft story justifies the price.

quiz.question: How long do Hermès artisans train before working on a Birkin?

details.summary: Hermès builds its entire brand narrative around craft: the hours spent hand-stitching a Birkin bag, the generations of artisans trained at the Hermès workshop, the scarcity created by human limitation rather than artificial restriction. details.whyItMatters: Hermès demonstrates that process can be more compelling than product. Telling the story of how something is made creates value that specifications alone cannot achieve.
takeaways: Hermès positions artisan craft as the core brand narrative
Process storytelling transforms products into objects of cultural value
Scarcity from genuine craftsmanship is more credible than artificial limits

faq.question: How does Hermès use craft in its copywriting?
faq.answer: By detailing specific processes: the 18 hours required to hand-stitch a Birkin bag, the years of training each artisan undergoes, the family workshops that have operated for generations. faq.question: Why is the craft narrative so persuasive?
faq.answer: Humans instinctively value things that took time, skill, and care to create. The 'IKEA effect' shows we even value things we built ourselves. Craft narratives tap into this bias, making buyers feel they are investing in human artistry rather than purchasing a commodity.
